rw: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage, including the interest rate plus certain fees, so shoppers can compare loan offers fairly under the Truth in Lending Act.

ww.The amount of the first monthly payment: The first monthly payment is a dollar amount set by the loan terms, while APR is an annual percentage rate that expresses yearly borrowing cost.
ww.The length of the loan measured in years: The loan term in years and months tells how long repayment lasts, but APR is a rate that measures the yearly cost of credit, not a time length.
ww.The total amount that was borrowed by th: The total amount borrowed is the principal of the loan, which is a dollar figure; APR is instead a percentage showing the annual cost of that credit.

rw: The ECOA prohibits credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age or receipt of public assistance, so lenders must judge applicants on creditworthiness.

ww.Requiring borrowers to repay their loans: Requiring on-time repayment is a normal and legal part of any loan agreement, and the ECOA does not prohibit lenders from expecting borrowers to pay as promised.
ww.Charging any amount of interest at all t: Charging interest is legal and is how lenders earn income; the ECOA bans discrimination, not interest, though usury laws and other rules may cap how high rates go.
ww.Checking a borrower's credit reports bef: Lenders are allowed and expected to check credit reports before lending, since that is how they judge risk; the ECOA only prohibits using protected traits to decide.

rw: The FDCPA bans abusive, deceptive and unfair practices by third-party debt collectors, such as harassing calls, threats, false statements and contacting people at unreasonable hours or places.

ww.The ability of banks to open new account: The FDCPA does not control how banks open accounts; it is a consumer protection law aimed at the behavior of third-party debt collectors, not at bank account opening.
ww.The ability of retailers to advertise go: Retail advertising is governed by other laws such as FTC rules on deceptive ads; the FDCPA deals only with how debt collectors contact and treat people who owe money.
ww.A borrower's right to repay a debt in fu: Borrowers always keep the right to repay a debt in full; the FDCPA protects consumers from collector abuse and does not limit anyone's ability to pay off what they owe.

rw: The FDCPA bars collectors from calling before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. and from threatening arrest or other action they cannot lawfully take, so this likely violates it.

ww.A protection under bankruptcy law: Bankruptcy law gives debtors an automatic stay that stops collection, but it does not authorize a collector to threaten arrest or call late at night.
ww.A needed part of the contract: A lawful contract does not allow a collector to harass or threaten the borrower, so harassment is never a needed part of a credit card agreement.
ww.A legal and normal collection step: Collectors may lawfully call and send letters, but threatening arrest for unpaid consumer debt and calling at odd hours are not legal or normal collection steps.

rw: Bankruptcy is a federal court process that lets people or businesses who cannot repay their debts either discharge many of them or set up a court-approved repayment plan.

ww.A tax paid only by wealthy individuals e: Bankruptcy is not a tax; it is a court proceeding about debts, and the wealthy are not the only ones who file, as most filers are ordinary consumers.
ww.A method of avoiding every kind of tax o: Bankruptcy does not erase every tax owed, and many recent income taxes are not discharged, so it is not a method for avoiding all taxes.
ww.A type of loan that businesses often tak: Bankruptcy is a legal proceeding rather than a loan; businesses may borrow money, but filing bankruptcy is what happens when debts cannot be repaid.

rw: In Chapter 7 a trustee sells the debtor's non-exempt assets to pay creditors, and remaining eligible debts are then discharged, which is why it is called liquidation bankruptcy.

ww.A program that offers a tax reduction to: Chapter 7 is not a tax reduction program; it is a court liquidation process, and it offers no yearly tax break to small filers.
ww.A repayment plan that lasts three to fiv: A three to five year repayment plan describes Chapter 13 for people with regular income, not Chapter 7, which ends quickly through a liquidation of assets.
ww.A reorganization plan that is meant only: Reorganization for businesses is the purpose of Chapter 11, and Chapter 7 is not limited to large firms because individuals and small businesses file it too.

rw: Chapter 11 lets a business keep operating while it restructures debts under a court-approved plan, and it is commonly used by companies that hope to return to profitability.

ww.Reducing the taxes owed by the business: Chapter 11 is a restructuring of business debts under court supervision, not a way to cut the owner's tax bill; taxes are handled separately.
ww.Closing a business down immediately for: Immediately closing a business and selling its assets describes Chapter 7 liquidation, whereas Chapter 11 is meant to keep the business running while debts are reorganized.
ww.A repayment plan meant for wage earners: A repayment plan for wage earners describes Chapter 13, while Chapter 11 is mainly used by businesses, though some individuals with large debts also use it.

rw: Chapter 13 lets individuals with regular income keep their property while repaying some or all debts through a three to five year plan approved by the bankruptcy court.

ww.A sale of all of a business's assets at: Selling all of a business's assets at once is liquidation, which describes Chapter 7 rather than Chapter 13, where the debtor generally keeps property while repaying.
ww.A tax audit process run by the IRS each: Chapter 13 is a bankruptcy proceeding in federal court and has nothing to do with an IRS tax audit, which is a review of a tax return.
ww.A reorganization meant for corporations: Corporations reorganize under Chapter 11, while Chapter 13 is limited to individuals with regular income and debts below set limits, so this does not describe it.

rw: The automatic stay temporarily halts most collection actions such as lawsuits, wage garnishment and foreclosure once a bankruptcy petition is filed, giving the debtor breathing room.

ww.Forces creditors to lend the debtor more: An automatic stay protects the debtor from collection efforts; it does not force creditors to make new loans or extend more credit to the debtor.
ww.Prevents the debtor from filing any taxe: Bankruptcy has no rule stopping the debtor from filing tax returns, and the stay deals with creditor collection actions rather than tax filing duties.
ww.Cancels all of the debtor's debts instan: The stay only pauses collection; debts are not canceled instantly or permanently, and cancellation of eligible debts comes later through a discharge order.

rw: A discharge is the court order that releases the debtor from personal liability for certain debts, so creditors can no longer try to collect them.

ww.A fine that is paid to the court clerk: A fine paid to the court clerk is a penalty, whereas a discharge is a court order that releases the debtor from personal liability for certain debts.
ww.A list of all of the creditors in a case: A list of creditors is filed in the case schedules, but a discharge is the court order that actually releases the debtor from certain listed debts.
ww.A new loan the court gives the borrower: A discharge is not a new loan; the court does not lend money, it simply relieves the debtor of obligation to pay certain debts.

rw: Most student loans and recent income taxes are generally not discharged, along with child support and alimony, so the debtor still owes them after bankruptcy.

ww.Medical bills from a hospital stay: Medical bills are unsecured debts that are generally dischargeable in bankruptcy, so they are not among the debts that typically survive a discharge.
ww.Credit card balances owed to a bank: Credit card balances are unsecured debts that are generally dischargeable, so bankruptcy can usually erase them, with limited exceptions for recent fraud or luxury purchases.
ww.Personal loans taken from a bank: Unsecured personal loans from a bank are generally dischargeable, so they typically are wiped out in bankruptcy unlike student loans or support obligations.

rw: A lien is a legal claim against property that secures payment of a debt, and the creditor can enforce it, for example by forcing a sale if the debt goes unpaid.

ww.A tax refund sent by the government: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer, whereas a lien is a claim a creditor places on property until a debt is paid.
ww.A written will that lists the heirs: A will is a document that lists heirs and directs distribution of property after death, while a lien is a creditor's claim against property for an unpaid debt.
ww.A free gift of property to a friend: Giving property to a friend freely is a gift, and a lien is the opposite because it attaches a creditor's claim to property.

rw: A mechanic's lien is a legal claim on property filed by a contractor or supplier who has not been paid for labor or materials used on it.

ww.A claim by a car owner on a mechanic: A car owner does not hold a mechanic's lien; the mechanic does, as a claim on the property they worked on when they are not paid.
ww.A warranty that comes with a car: A warranty is a promise about repair quality or coverage, while a mechanic's lien is a legal claim to secure payment for work that was done.
ww.A tax that is charged on repair shops: A mechanic's lien is not a tax on repair shops; it is a claim filed by a worker or supplier, not collected by a government.

rw: Garnishment is a court-ordered process where an employer withholds part of wages and sends it to a creditor, such as for unpaid debts, child support or taxes.

ww.A voluntary savings plan the worker choo: Garnishment is not voluntary; the worker does not choose it, and it is ordered by a court or agency to repay a debt rather than to build savings.
ww.A tax refund the worker receives each ye: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer, whereas garnishment takes money out of the worker's pay to satisfy a debt.
ww.A bonus that is paid to employees each y: A bonus adds to pay, but garnishment reduces take-home pay because a court orders part of wages to be sent to a creditor.

rw: A mortgage is a loan secured by real estate, so the lender can foreclose and sell the property if the borrower stops making payments.

ww.A type of insurance policy: Insurance is a contract paying for losses, while a mortgage is a loan; though lenders may require homeowner's insurance, the mortgage itself is a loan secured by property.
ww.An unsecured loan from a bank: A mortgage is a secured loan because the property is collateral, so it is not an unsecured loan, which has no collateral behind it.
ww.A loan secured by a car title: A loan secured by a car title is an auto loan, whereas a mortgage uses real estate as collateral for the money borrowed.

rw: Foreclosure is the legal process a lender uses to take and sell a property after the borrower defaults on a mortgage, using sale proceeds to repay the debt.

ww.A bank's approval of a new loan to a hom: Approving a new loan is underwriting, and foreclosure happens later when a borrower defaults, so it is not a loan approval.
ww.The sale of a home by choice with no deb: A voluntary sale with no debt owed is an ordinary home sale, while foreclosure is forced by the lender because the borrower failed to pay.
ww.A tax credit that is given to homeowners: A tax credit reduces taxes owed and has nothing to do with foreclosure, which is how a lender takes a home after missed payments.

rw: RESPA requires lenders to disclose closing costs and settlement services to home buyers and bans kickbacks and referral fees, helping buyers compare offers and avoid hidden charges.

ww.Bans every kind of closing fee at all: RESPA does not ban closing fees; it requires lenders to disclose them and prohibits kickbacks, while fees themselves remain a normal part of buying a home.
ww.Guarantees that a buyer gets a mortgage: RESPA does not guarantee a buyer approval; lenders still decide whether to lend based on credit, income and other qualifications of the borrower.
ww.Sets the prices that homes may sell for: Home prices are set by the market of buyers and sellers, and RESPA does not regulate what price a house can sell for.

rw: Usury laws set a legal maximum interest rate that lenders may charge, protecting borrowers from excessively high or predatory rates, and the limits vary by state.

ww.A law that requires banks to lend more a: Usury laws restrict lending rates and do not require banks to lend more; they limit how much interest a lender can charge, not how much they must lend.
ww.A law that sets minimum interest rates f: Usury laws cap the highest rate allowed rather than set a minimum rate, so they protect borrowers and do not set a floor for lenders.
ww.A law that bans savings accounts at all: Usury laws concern the interest rates charged on loans and do not ban savings accounts, which banks are free to offer.

rw: The FDIC is an independent federal agency created in 1933 that insures bank deposits up to a set limit, which protects customers if a bank fails.

ww.An agency that regulates stocks and bond: Regulating the stock and bond markets is the job of the Securities and Exchange Commission, not the FDIC, whose focus is insuring bank deposits.
ww.An agency that collects the income taxes: The IRS collects federal income taxes owed by workers, while the FDIC has nothing to do with taxes and instead insures bank deposits.
ww.A private lender that makes loans to fir: The FDIC is a government agency, not a private lender, and it does not make loans to firms and homes; it insures bank deposits.

rw: The standard FDIC insurance amount is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, so deposits above that at one bank in one category may be at risk.

ww.$1,000,000: One million dollars is not the standard limit; coverage can reach more only by using different ownership categories or banks, since the base limit is $250,000.
ww.$25,000: The $25,000 amount is far below the actual coverage limit, which was raised over time and now stands at $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per category.
ww.$100: One hundred dollars is not an FDIC insurance limit at all; the actual standard coverage amount is $250,000 for each depositor, bank and ownership category.

rw: The SEC regulates securities markets, enforces laws against fraud and insider trading, and requires public companies to disclose financial information so investors can make informed choices.

ww.Highway traffic and road safety for driv: Highway traffic and driver safety are handled by agencies such as the Department of Transportation, while the SEC regulates securities markets and company disclosures.
ww.Workplace safety inside factories and pl: Workplace safety in factories is overseen by OSHA, a different agency, while the SEC concerns itself with securities and investor protection.
ww.Public schools and their funding sources: Public schools are funded and run by state and local governments and the Department of Education, not by the SEC, which regulates securities markets.

rw: Insider trading is buying or selling securities using material non-public information, which is illegal because it gives some traders an unfair advantage over other investors.

ww.A broker placing a customer's trade orde: A broker placing a customer's order is ordinary legal market activity, whereas insider trading involves using material non-public information to trade securities.
ww.Trading stock using only public informat: Trading on public information from the news is legal, since everyone has access to it, whereas insider trading depends on information the public does not have.
ww.Employees buying their own company's pro: Employees buying products at a discount is a normal workplace benefit and has nothing to do with trading securities based on confidential information.

rw: Trading stock on confidential knowledge of an upcoming acquisition is illegal insider trading, because the information is material and not yet public, and it is punishable by the SEC.

ww.Legal diversification: Diversification means spreading investments across assets to reduce risk, not buying one stock based on secret information about a pending deal.
ww.Normal market research: Market research relies on public information, whereas buying stock because of a private tip about an acquisition is not research but an unfair advantage.
ww.A permitted benefit: Employees are not permitted to trade on confidential company news, so this is not a benefit but rather a violation of securities laws.

rw: Sarbanes-Oxley requires public companies to keep stronger internal controls and report accurately, with executives certifying financial statements, after scandals like Enron and WorldCom.

ww.Lower tax rates for public companies: Sarbanes-Oxley does not change tax rates; it was passed in 2002 after accounting scandals to improve corporate governance and financial reporting.
ww.Paying dividends to investors every year: Public companies are not required by Sarbanes-Oxley to pay dividends; dividends are a board decision, while the Act focuses on financial controls and accuracy.
ww.Free stock for every employee of the fir: Giving every employee free stock is not something Sarbanes-Oxley requires, as the law concerns reporting accuracy, internal controls and auditor independence.

rw: A tax is a mandatory payment to government, imposed by law, that funds public services such as roads, schools and defense, whether or not the payer uses them directly.

ww.A loan that is made to the government: A loan to the government is lending money that gets repaid, such as buying a bond, while a tax is a required payment that does not have to be repaid.
ww.A fee for a private service from a compa: A fee for a private service from a company is a price paid in the marketplace, while a tax is imposed by government and funds public services.
ww.A voluntary donation to a charity by a c: Taxes are mandatory, not voluntary, so a voluntary donation to charity does not fit the legal definition of a tax.

rw: A progressive tax system charges higher rates as income rises, so people with more income pay a larger percentage, as in the US federal income tax brackets.

ww.Lower incomes are taxed at higher rates: Taxing lower incomes at higher rates describes a regressive pattern, which is the reverse of a progressive system where the rate rises with income.
ww.All incomes are taxed at the same rate: Taxing all incomes at the same rate describes a flat or proportional tax, not a progressive one, in which rates increase with income.
ww.Only corporations pay any tax at all: In a progressive system individuals pay tax too; it is not limited to corporations, and progressive refers to rates rising with income.

rw: A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from lower earners than from higher earners, as with sales taxes that weigh more heavily on those with low incomes.

ww.A tax that no one pays, as it was abolis: A regressive tax is still collected, so a tax that was abolished and that no one pays is not a regressive tax at all.
ww.A tax that is the same percent of income: Taking the same percentage of income from everyone describes a proportional or flat tax, not a regressive tax, which takes a larger share from lower earners.
ww.A tax that takes more from higher earner: Taking more from higher earners describes a progressive tax, which is the opposite of a regressive tax that falls harder on low-income people.

rw: The Internal Revenue Service, part of the Treasury Department, collects federal income taxes and administers the tax code, including processing returns and refunds.

ww.The Federal Trade Commission (FTC): The Federal Trade Commission handles consumer protection and competition issues, not federal income tax collection, which belongs to the IRS.
ww.The Securities and Exchange Commission: The Securities and Exchange Commission regulates securities markets and does not collect income taxes from workers or businesses.
ww.The Federal Reserve Board of Governors: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and supervises banks, but it does not collect income taxes from the public.

rw: Tax withholding means an employer deducts income tax from each paycheck and sends it to the government, so taxes are paid gradually throughout the year.

ww.A business keeping its tax money until y: Withholding is not a business holding tax money until year end; employers must send withheld taxes to the government regularly, often every pay period or monthly.
ww.A penalty for lateness in filing a tax r: A penalty for filing late is a separate charge; withholding is an ordinary pay deduction, not a punishment for lateness.
ww.A bonus given to employees at the end of: Withholding reduces take-home pay rather than adding to it, so it is the opposite of a year-end bonus given to employees.

rw: Filing late without an extension can bring a failure-to-file penalty and a failure-to-pay penalty plus interest, so the cost grows the longer the return and payment are late.

ww.Lower taxes next year for filing late: Filing late does not lower taxes next year; late filers without an extension face penalties and interest that increase what they owe.
ww.A tax refund bonus for filing late: Filing late does not earn a refund bonus; any refund is only what was overpaid, and late filing may even forfeit it after three years.
ww.No consequence at all for late filers: Late filers do face consequences, because the IRS charges penalties and interest on unpaid tax, so claiming no consequence is wrong.

rw: Tax evasion is the illegal act of hiding income or lying on a return to cut taxes owed, and it can bring fines and prison.

ww.Using legal deductions to cut a tax bill: Using legal deductions to cut a tax bill is tax avoidance, which is lawful, whereas evasion means deliberately breaking the law to pay less.
ww.Filing a correct return right on time: Filing a correct return on time is honest compliance, which is the opposite of evasion, where income is hidden or falsified.
ww.Paying estimated taxes each quarter: Paying estimated taxes each quarter is lawful and often required for the self-employed, so it is compliance rather than evasion.

rw: A sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and some services at the time of purchase and collected by the seller for the state or locality.

ww.A tax on houses and other land: A tax on houses and land is a property tax, which is based on assessed value rather than on a purchase at checkout.
ww.A tax on inherited property at death: A tax on inherited property at death is an estate or inheritance tax, which is different from the tax added to purchases.
ww.A tax on wages and other salaries: A tax on wages and salaries is an income or payroll tax, not a sales tax, which applies when buying goods.

rw: A use tax is owed on goods bought out of state, such as online without sales tax, then used in your home state, so it matches the sales tax you would have paid.

ww.A tax on using a bank or a credit union: There is no standard tax on using a bank or credit union; a use tax applies to goods bought without sales tax and then used in the state.
ww.A tax on using public roads, paid on fue: A tax on fuel for using public roads is a fuel or excise tax, which is different from a use tax on purchased goods.
ww.A tax on leased cars only, not bought on: A use tax is not limited to leased cars; it applies to many purchased items brought into a state without sales tax having been paid.

rw: A property tax is based on the assessed value of real estate, which local governments multiply by a tax rate to fund services such as schools and roads.

ww.The wages earned by the home owner: Property tax is based on the value of property owned, not on the wages the owner earns, which are taxed through income tax instead.
ww.The number of employees at the firm: The number of employees at a firm affects payroll taxes, but property tax depends on the assessed value of land and buildings.
ww.The price of goods sold last year: Sales tax depends on the price of goods sold, but property tax is based on assessed value of real estate rather than past sales.

rw: An estate tax is imposed on the transfer of a deceased person's property to heirs, typically only when the estate is larger than a high exemption amount.

ww.A tax on buying real estate, paid at clo: A tax on buying real estate at closing is a transfer or recording tax, while the estate tax is levied on property passed at death.
ww.A tax on rental income earned by a landl: A tax on a landlord's rental income is part of income tax, which differs from an estate tax levied when someone dies.
ww.A tax on selling a business to a new own: Selling a business may trigger capital gains tax, whereas an estate tax applies to the transfer of property when its owner dies.

rw: A payroll tax is a tax on wages paid by employers and employees, funding programs such as Social Security and Medicare, and is usually withheld from each paycheck.

ww.A tax on land and the buildings on it: A tax on land and buildings is a property tax, which is based on assessed real estate value instead of on wages paid.
ww.A tax on gifts given to another person: A tax on gifts is a gift tax, paid by the giver in some cases, which differs from a payroll tax on wages.
ww.A tax on purchases made at retail stores: A tax on purchases at retail stores is a sales tax, not a payroll tax, which is based on wages earned by employees.

rw: FICA stands for Federal Insurance Contributions Act and covers Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, split between employee and employer at 7.65% each.

ww.Taxes on stock gains and dividends: Taxes on stock gains and dividends are capital gains and income taxes, whereas FICA taxes are payroll taxes taken from wages.
ww.Taxes on imported goods paid at ports: Taxes on imported goods are called tariffs or customs duties, which are unrelated to FICA payroll taxes taken from wages.
ww.Taxes on property and land owned: Taxes on property and land are property taxes levied locally, while FICA taxes are federal payroll taxes on earnings.

rw: Multiply $4,000 by 0.0765 and you get $306, so that is the monthly FICA tax withheld from the employee's pay.

ww.$612: $612 is double the correct amount of $306, which would be the employee plus employer share combined, but the question asks only for the employee's withholding.
ww.$3,060: $3,060 is ten times too large, caused by misplacing the decimal point; the correct calculation is $4,000 x 0.0765 = $306.
ww.$30.60: $30.60 is ten times too small, caused by a decimal error; 7.65% of $4,000 is $306, not $30.60.

rw: A tax deduction is an amount subtracted from income before tax is calculated, which lowers taxable income, and its value depends on the taxpayer's tax bracket.

ww.A refund from a bank paid to the account: A refund from a bank is not a tax deduction; a deduction is an amount subtracted from income to reduce taxable income before tax is computed.
ww.An added penalty on top of the tax that: An added penalty on top of tax owed is a penalty or interest charge, not a deduction, which reduces the income that gets taxed.
ww.An amount subtracted directly from the t: An amount subtracted directly from the tax after it is calculated describes a tax credit, which reduces tax dollar for dollar, unlike a deduction.

rw: Ordinary and necessary business costs, such as rent, supplies, wages and advertising, are generally deductible because they are common in the trade and help the business operate.

ww.Personal vacations for the owner: Personal vacations for the owner are personal expenses, not business costs, so the IRS does not allow them as business deductions.
ww.Fines for breaking the law or rules: Fines for breaking the law are generally not deductible, because tax law does not let businesses reduce taxes with penalties for wrongdoing.
ww.The owner's groceries and meals: The owner's groceries and personal meals are personal living costs, so they are not deductible as ordinary business expenses.

rw: By default an LLC is a pass-through entity, so profits are taxed once on the owners' personal returns, though it may elect to be taxed as a corporation.

ww.A company that pays no taxes, as its own: An LLC does not simply pay no taxes; by default its income passes through to the owners, who report and pay tax on their own returns.
ww.A nonprofit that pays no taxes on its in: An LLC is a for-profit business structure, not a nonprofit, and it is not automatically exempt from tax on its income.
ww.A government agency that collects the ta: An LLC is a private business entity formed under state law and has no power to collect taxes, which governments do.

rw: A tax audit is an IRS examination of a return to verify accuracy, whereas a tax lien is a legal claim against property for unpaid taxes.

ww.An audit is a bank loan; a lien is a ref: A tax audit is an IRS review and is not a bank loan, while a lien is a legal claim on property rather than a refund.
ww.Both are rewards for filing early each y: Neither is a reward; an audit is a review of a return and a lien is a claim, and filing early earns neither of them.
ww.Both mean exactly the same thing in tax: The two terms mean different things in tax law, since an audit examines a return while a lien secures the government's claim for unpaid tax.

rw: A tax-exempt organization is exempt from certain taxes, such as federal income tax, because of its purpose, and charities and educational groups are common examples.

ww.A group that has no members and no asset: A tax-exempt organization can have members and assets, and being exempt refers to certain taxes rather than to having no members or assets.
ww.A business that never files forms with t: Tax-exempt groups still must file forms such as the IRS Form 990, so it is false that they never file with the state or IRS.
ww.A government office that sells bonds to: A government office selling bonds is a government function, while a tax-exempt organization is typically a private nonprofit exempt from certain taxes.

rw: Section 501(c)(3) covers charitable, religious, educational, scientific and similar organizations, which are exempt from federal income tax and can receive tax-deductible donations.

ww.For-profit manufacturers and retail firm: For-profit manufacturers and retail firms pay taxes on profits and are not covered by section 501(c)(3), which is for organizations serving public purposes.
ww.Foreign governments and their agencies a: Foreign governments are not 501(c)(3) organizations, as that section applies to domestic charitable and educational groups, not foreign government agencies.
ww.Political campaigns and the parties they: Political campaigns and parties are covered by other sections of the code, since 501(c)(3) groups are restricted from supporting candidates.

rw: An IRS installment agreement lets a taxpayer who cannot pay in full pay the tax debt in monthly payments over time, though interest and penalties continue to accrue.

ww.A refund paid in monthly parts: An installment agreement is a payment plan for taxes owed, not a refund, so it does not pay a refund to the taxpayer in parts.
ww.A penalty doubled each month: An installment agreement does not double penalties each month; it lets a taxpayer pay a debt over time, though interest and penalties still accrue.
ww.A rule that cancels the debt: An installment agreement does not cancel the debt, since the taxpayer still owes the full amount; the plan simply spreads payments out.

rw: Identity theft is using another person's personal data, such as a Social Security number or card number, without permission to commit fraud or other crimes.

ww.Forgetting your own password for a websi: Forgetting your own password is an access problem and not identity theft, since no one else has taken or misused your personal information.
ww.Checking your own credit report once a y: Checking your own credit report once a year is a smart habit for spotting fraud and is not itself identity theft.
ww.Updating your address with the bank afte: Updating your address with your bank after a move is a normal account update that you authorize, not identity theft.

rw: After discovering identity theft, place a fraud alert or credit freeze with the credit bureaus and report it to the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov to limit further damage.

ww.Post the details publicly on social medi: Posting details publicly on social media would expose more personal data and help thieves rather than limit the harm.
ww.Wait several months to see what will hap: Waiting for months lets the thief open more accounts and run up debts, so quick action is needed to contain the damage.
ww.Share your password with the caller from: Sharing your password with a caller is how thieves gain access, and a real bank never asks customers for their passwords by phone.

rw: Business ethics are principles of right and wrong that guide how companies and employees behave, going beyond what the law merely requires.

ww.Laws passed by the legislature each year: Laws are rules set by the legislature and enforced by the government, whereas ethics are moral principles that apply even where no law exists.
ww.Rules that only apply to large firms: Business ethics apply to firms of every size, including small shops and sole proprietors, and not only to large corporations.
ww.A list of company profit targets for the: Profit targets are financial goals set by management, whereas business ethics concern moral principles of right and wrong in how goals are pursued.

rw: Telling customers the truth about a product's limits is honest and ethical, builds trust, and helps buyers make informed choices.

ww.Overcharging customers who ask few quest: Overcharging customers who do not ask about price takes unfair advantage of them, which is unethical even if it is not always illegal.
ww.Hiding defects from buyers in order to m: Hiding defects from buyers is deceptive and unethical, and it can also violate consumer protection laws and lead to lawsuits.
ww.Copying a competitor's secret formula fo: Copying a competitor's secret formula is theft of a trade secret, which is both unethical and illegal.

rw: Integrity means being honest and holding to strong moral principles, doing the right thing even when no one is watching or would find out.

ww.Following orders without question: Following orders without question can lead to wrongdoing, so it is obedience rather than integrity, which relies on one's own moral principles.
ww.Doing whatever pays the most at the time: Doing whatever pays the most at the time puts money ahead of principles, which is the opposite of acting with integrity.
ww.Avoiding every risk in every case: Avoiding every risk is caution, not integrity, since people with integrity may still take risks when it is the right thing to do.

rw: A conflict of interest arises when personal interests, such as finances or family ties, could interfere with a person's duty to act in the employer's best interest.

ww.A debate about company slogans and new l: A debate about slogans and logos is a marketing disagreement and does not involve personal interests clashing with duties to the employer.
ww.A disagreement over office furniture or: A disagreement over office furniture or temperature is a workplace preference issue and does not involve a conflict between personal and professional duties.
ww.A competition between two stores in the: Competition between two stores is normal business rivalry, whereas a conflict of interest involves one person's personal interests clashing with duties they owe.

rw: Secretly giving a contract to the manager's brother's firm is a conflict of interest, because family ties could override the duty to pick the best supplier and should have been disclosed.

ww.Good teamwork skills: Awarding a contract to a relative in secret is not teamwork; it is self-dealing that favors personal ties over the company's interests.
ww.A routine hiring plan: Hiring plans follow open procedures, but this case involves a hidden personal relationship affecting a contract, which is not routine hiring.
ww.Fair open competition: Fair competition means suppliers are judged on merit through an open process, while a secret award to family bypasses that fairness.

rw: The best way to handle a conflict of interest is to disclose it to the employer and recuse yourself from the decision so that it remains fair.

ww.Ask a friend to decide in secret for the: Asking a friend to decide in secret still hides the conflict and does not remove the problem, because the firm is not told about it.
ww.Make the decision anyway and say nothing: Deciding anyway and saying nothing leaves the conflict undisclosed and lets personal interest influence the decision, which is the very problem to avoid.
ww.Hide it and hope that no one ever notice: Hiding a conflict and hoping no one notices is dishonest, and it often leads to discipline or legal trouble when discovered.

rw: A bribe is something of value, such as money or gifts, offered to improperly influence someone's decision or official action, and bribery is illegal.

ww.A thank-you card sent to a customer afte: A thank-you card after a job is a harmless courtesy with no value offered to influence a decision, so it is not a bribe.
ww.A legal discount for bulk orders from a: A legal volume discount is openly offered to buyers as a pricing policy and does not secretly sway a decision, so it is not a bribe.
ww.A fair commission for a sale made by an: A fair commission paid to an agent for a sale is lawful compensation within an agreement, not something offered to corruptly influence someone.

rw: Refusing the offer and reporting it keeps the buyer honest and protects the company, since a luxury trip in exchange for a contract is a bribe.

ww.Ask for an even better trip: Asking for an even better trip would be soliciting a bribe, which is itself unethical and likely illegal for the buyer.
ww.Accept it quietly and keep it: Accepting the trip quietly is taking a bribe and hides a conflict of interest, which is unethical and can lead to firing or prosecution.
ww.Accept it but pick the best bid: Even if the bid is the best one, accepting the trip is still taking a bribe and creates an appearance of corruption.

rw: A gift policy sets limits on gifts given and received so that they cannot influence business decisions or create the appearance of bribery.

ww.Ban all thanks from staff to customers: A gift policy does not ban all thanks; it sets reasonable limits, so small tokens can still be allowed while large gifts that could sway judgment are restricted.
ww.Promote secret gift exchanges among staf: Gift policies require openness and are meant to prevent secret exchanges, which could hide improper influence on decisions.
ww.Require gifts to be expensive each year: A gift policy limits expensive gifts rather than requiring them, since costly gifts are more likely to sway business decisions.

rw: Whistleblowing is reporting illegal or unethical conduct within an organization to management or authorities, and laws protect whistleblowers from retaliation in many cases.

ww.Quitting without notice to the boss: Quitting without notice is leaving a job abruptly, while whistleblowing is reporting wrongdoing to someone who can address it.
ww.Spreading false rumors about a coworker: Spreading false rumors is gossip or defamation, whereas whistleblowing involves truthfully reporting actual misconduct.
ww.Asking for a raise from your manager: Asking for a raise is a pay negotiation and has nothing to do with reporting misconduct, which is what whistleblowing means.

rw: Anonymous hotlines let employees report possible misconduct without fear of retaliation, which helps companies catch problems early and build an ethical culture.

ww.To advertise products to new customers: Advertising to customers is a marketing function, while an ethics hotline is an internal tool for staff to report concerns.
ww.To replace the legal department staff: A hotline does not replace the legal department, which handles legal work; it only gives employees a channel for reporting concerns.
ww.To track employee phone usage at work: Monitoring phone usage is a different workplace practice, while an ethics hotline exists to let staff raise concerns about misconduct.

rw: A code of conduct is a written set of rules and standards describing the behavior a company expects from employees, covering topics such as honesty and conflicts of interest.

ww.A tax form used for yearly returns: A tax form used for yearly returns, like Form 1040, is a government document, while a code of conduct is an internal company document.
ww.A secret list of passwords for staff: A code of conduct is shared openly with staff, while a secret list of passwords would be a security risk and is not a code of conduct.
ww.A list of products on sale today: A list of products on sale is marketing information, whereas a code of conduct sets standards for how employees should behave.

rw: Corporate social responsibility means a company acts to benefit society and the environment, beyond profit and legal minimums, through things like community support and sustainable practices.

ww.A way to avoid regulation by the governm: CSR is not a way to avoid regulation; companies still have to follow the law, and CSR goes beyond legal minimums.
ww.A tax strategy to lower the yearly tax b: CSR is not a tax strategy, although some CSR spending, such as charitable gifts, may be deductible as a side effect.
ww.A requirement to give away all profits e: CSR does not require giving away all profits; companies choose to contribute while remaining profitable enough to operate.

rw: Cutting packaging waste and supporting charities are voluntary actions that benefit society and the environment, which is what corporate social responsibility means.

ww.Hiding safety problems from the buying p: Hiding safety problems from the public is unethical and often illegal, so it is the opposite of social responsibility.
ww.Ignoring community concerns to protect p: Ignoring community concerns to protect profits puts money ahead of society, which does not reflect corporate social responsibility.
ww.Dumping waste to cut costs at the plant: Dumping waste to cut costs harms the environment and the community, which is the opposite of social responsibility and may be illegal.

rw: Greenwashing is making misleading or false claims that a product or company is environmentally friendly, which can violate FTC rules on deceptive advertising.

ww.Recycling packaging properly at the plan: Properly recycling packaging is a real environmental practice, whereas greenwashing involves making misleading environmental claims.
ww.Publishing a true sustainability report: Publishing a true sustainability report is honest disclosure, while greenwashing involves exaggerating or faking environmental claims.
ww.Planting trees at a company office: Planting trees at an office is a real environmental action and not greenwashing unless the company misrepresents its impact.

rw: Being accountable means owning your actions and their results, admitting mistakes and taking responsibility for fixing them.

ww.Hiding errors from managers and staff: Hiding errors from managers and staff avoids responsibility, so it is the opposite of being accountable.
ww.Ignoring feedback from your colleagues: Ignoring feedback from colleagues avoids learning and responsibility, which does not show accountability.
ww.Blaming others for all of your mistakes: Blaming others for your own mistakes avoids responsibility, so it is the opposite of accountability.

rw: Transparency means being open and honest about decisions, practices and results so that stakeholders can understand and trust the organization.

ww.Sharing only good news with the public: Sharing only good news hides problems and gives a one-sided picture, so it is not transparency, which includes the bad news too.
ww.Using clear windows in the office: Transparent in business is a figure of speech about openness and does not refer to office windows or building design.
ww.Hiding information from the public alway: Hiding information from the public always is secrecy, which is the opposite of transparency.

rw: Stakeholder theory holds that a company should consider the interests of everyone affected by its actions, including employees, customers, suppliers, communities and owners.

ww.Only employees matter to the business: Stakeholder theory does not say only employees matter; it includes many groups, and employees are just one of them.
ww.Only the government matters in the end: Stakeholder theory does not say only the government matters, as the government is just one of many stakeholders.
ww.Only shareholders matter, as they own it: Saying only shareholders matter is the shareholder view, which differs from stakeholder theory that weighs all affected groups.

rw: Stakeholders are individuals or groups affected by a business's actions, such as employees, customers, suppliers, investors and communities.

ww.Only the government and its agencies: Stakeholders are not limited to the government; they include any group affected by the business, such as customers and employees.
ww.Only the owners, since none else cares: Stakeholders include more than owners, because employees, customers, suppliers and communities are also affected by what a business does.
ww.Only the competitors of the company: Competitors are only one possible stakeholder group; the term stakeholders covers all groups with an interest in the business.

rw: The shareholder view, associated with Milton Friedman, says a business's responsibility is to increase owners' value while obeying the law and ethical custom.

ww.A company must serve all stakeholders: Serving all stakeholders is the stakeholder view, whereas the shareholder view says a company's main duty is to its owners.
ww.A company must avoid making any profit: The shareholder view encourages profit within the law, so it does not say a company must avoid making any profit.
ww.A company should ignore all the laws: Even the shareholder view says a company should follow the law, so ignoring the law is not part of it.

rw: A stakeholder-focused manager weighs worker safety and community risk against costs, since people affected by the decision count even when the law does not demand the upgrade.

ww.Reduce workers' pay instead of paying fo: Cutting workers' pay to avoid paying for safety shifts the cost onto employees, which a stakeholder-focused manager would see as unfair to workers.
ww.Hide the risk from workers and from the: Hiding the risk from workers and the public would harm stakeholders and break trust, so a stakeholder-focused manager would not do it.
ww.Skip the upgrade because no law or rule: Skipping the upgrade only because no law requires it reflects a shareholder or legalistic view, which ignores harm to other stakeholders.

rw: An ethical dilemma is a hard choice in which values or obligations conflict, so no option is fully right and every choice has a cost.

ww.A choice with an obvious answer and no c: A choice with an obvious answer and no conflict is a simple decision, not a dilemma, which involves competing values.
ww.A decision made by a computer program al: A decision made by a computer program alone does not define a dilemma; what matters is a conflict between ethical values.
ww.A mistake in a financial statement for t: A mistake in a financial statement is an accounting error, while an ethical dilemma is a hard choice between competing values.

rw: Asking whether you would be fine if the decision were made public is a classic ethics test, because it checks if you could defend your actions openly.

ww.Will anyone notice if I do this thing?: Asking whether anyone will notice focuses on avoiding detection and not on whether the action is right, so it is a poor ethics test.
ww.Is this the cheapest option available to: Asking whether an option is the cheapest looks only at cost, so it does not test whether the decision is ethical.
ww.Can I blame someone else if it fails?: Asking whether you can blame someone else focuses on dodging responsibility, which is the opposite of an ethical test.

rw: A fiduciary duty is a legal and ethical duty to act in another party's best interest, as when trustees, agents, financial advisors or directors manage others' money.

ww.A duty to avoid paying any taxes owed: A fiduciary duty does not mean avoiding taxes; it means acting in the best interest of another person or entity.
ww.A duty to maximize personal pay and bonu: Fiduciaries must put others' interests ahead of their own pay and bonuses, so maximizing personal pay is not the duty.
ww.A duty to advertise to all new clients: Advertising is a marketing activity, whereas a fiduciary duty is a legal obligation to act in another party's best interest.

rw: Insider information is private company news not yet made public that could affect the stock price, and trading on it is illegal.

ww.Information in a newspaper or a magazine: Information in a newspaper or magazine is public, so anyone can legally act on it, unlike insider information.
ww.Information on the company website for a: Information posted on a company website for all is public, so it is not insider information.
ww.Information posted in a public press rel: A public press release is released to everyone, so it does not count as insider information.

rw: Plagiarism is presenting another person's work or ideas as your own without credit, which is dishonest and can lead to penalties or lost jobs.

ww.Quoting with permission from the author: Quoting with the author's permission is allowed and honest, so it is not plagiarism.
ww.Writing your own report from scratch: Writing your own report from scratch produces original work, which is the opposite of plagiarism.
ww.Citing a source with the author's name: Citing a source with the author's name gives credit where it is due, so it is the correct way to avoid plagiarism.

rw: Changing sales numbers to meet a target falsifies records by recording untrue figures to mislead others, which is unethical and may be fraud.

ww.Filing an accurate report right on time: Filing an accurate report on time is honest record keeping, so it is not falsifying records.
ww.Asking a coworker for help with a report: Asking a coworker for help with a report is normal collaboration and does not involve changing facts or records.
ww.Correcting a typing error openly with a: Correcting a typing error openly with a note is honest, because the change is disclosed, so it is not falsifying.

rw: You should decline to backdate the contract and raise the matter through proper channels, such as a compliance officer or hotline, since backdating misstates revenue.

ww.Backdate it, since the manager is in cha: Following a manager's order does not excuse fraud, because backdating a contract falsifies records and employees remain responsible for their actions.
ww.Backdate it but tell nobody about the ch: Backdating quietly is still falsifying records, and keeping it secret adds concealment to the wrongdoing.
ww.Delete the contract and tell nobody at a: Deleting the contract and telling nobody destroys records, which is another form of misconduct and does not address the problem.

rw: Workplace discrimination is treating people unfairly because of a protected trait such as race, sex, religion, age, disability or national origin, and it violates civil rights laws.

ww.Rewarding top performance with bonuses e: Rewarding top performance with bonuses is based on merit, not on a protected trait, so it is not discrimination.
ww.Choosing workers by age or gender, not s: Choosing workers by age or gender rather than skills is discrimination, but the correct answer defines it more generally as unfair treatment over a protected trait.
ww.Following the dress code set by the comp: Following a dress code that applies to everyone is a neutral policy and is not discrimination unless it targets a protected group.

rw: The main goal is a fair, welcoming workplace where people from varied backgrounds can contribute and succeed, which also improves ideas and morale.

ww.To lower hiring standards to fill open j: Diversity programs do not aim to lower hiring standards; they aim to widen the pool and ensure fair chances for qualified people.
ww.To avoid all training for the whole staf: Diversity and inclusion programs rely on training, so avoiding training is not their goal.
ww.To limit employee voices at the company: Limiting employee voices is the opposite of inclusion, which aims to hear and value many perspectives.

rw: Customer privacy means protecting customers' personal information from misuse or unauthorized access and using it only for the purposes they agreed to.

ww.Selling customer data to anyone who asks: Selling customer data to anyone who pays violates customer privacy, because it treats personal information as a product without consent.
ww.Sharing passwords with partners and outs: Sharing passwords with partners and outside firms exposes customer accounts to misuse, which breaks privacy rather than protecting it.
ww.Posting customers' details online for al: Posting customers' details online for all to see exposes personal data, which is the opposite of protecting privacy.

rw: Selling customers' emails without telling them breaks their trust and can violate privacy laws and the store's own policy, so it is unethical and possibly illegal.

ww.A required practice that all stores foll: Selling an email list without telling customers is not required, and many stores follow privacy policies that protect customer information.
ww.Good customer service for the buyer: Selling customer data without consent is not good customer service, since customers expected emails only for receipts.
ww.A neutral data practice with no harm: Selling personal data without consent can lead to spam and fraud, so it is not harmless or neutral.

rw: Deceptive advertising uses false, misleading or unsupported claims to persuade consumers, and the FTC can penalize it.

ww.Advertising with a coupon for savings: Advertising a coupon with real savings is honest promotion, so it is not deceptive advertising.
ww.Advertising on social media sites: Advertising on social media is simply a channel and is not deceptive unless the content itself misleads consumers.
ww.Advertising that is honest and clear: Honest and clear advertising tells the truth about a product, so it is the opposite of deceptive advertising.

rw: The FTC enforces laws against unfair or deceptive advertising and can act against unproven health claims like this one, requiring evidence to back them up.

The National Park Service manages parks and historic sites, so it has no authority over health claims in advertising.
ww.The Social Security Administration: The Social Security Administration runs retirement and disability benefits and does not regulate advertising claims.
ww.The Federal Reserve Bank system: The Federal Reserve oversees monetary policy and banks, not advertising claims about health products.

rw: Bait-and-switch lures buyers with an attractive low price on an item that is unavailable, then pushes a more expensive one, and it is a deceptive practice.

ww.Giving a full refund to unhappy customer: Giving refunds to unhappy customers is good service, while bait-and-switch involves luring customers with an offer the seller does not intend to honor.
ww.Switching to a new brand name openly wit: Openly switching brand names with a notice is honest, whereas bait-and-switch deceives customers about what is being offered.
ww.Offering a legitimate sale to all buyers: A legitimate sale offered to all buyers honors the advertised price, so it is not bait-and-switch.

rw: Price gouging is charging unfairly high prices during an emergency or shortage, such as raising bottled water prices after a hurricane, and many states ban it.

ww.Posting prices clearly on each item: Posting prices clearly is good practice and is not gouging, which means raising prices unfairly.
ww.Matching a competitor's price on goods: Matching a competitor's price is ordinary competition, whereas gouging is charging excessive prices when buyers have no alternatives.
ww.Lowering prices during a short sale: Lowering prices during a sale benefits buyers and is the opposite of gouging.

rw: A monopoly is a market dominated by a single seller with little or no competition, which can let it control prices and output.

ww.A group of buyers who buy together: A group of buyers purchasing together is a buying cooperative or group, not a monopoly, which is about a single seller.
ww.A market with many equal sellers: A market with many equal sellers describes perfect competition, which is the opposite of a monopoly.
ww.A store owned by the government only: A government-owned store may be a public enterprise, but a monopoly is defined by one seller dominating a market, not by government ownership.

rw: Price fixing is when competitors agree to set prices rather than compete, which is illegal under antitrust laws such as the Sherman Act.

ww.A store cutting its own price: A store cutting its own price is independent competition, which is legal, whereas price fixing requires an agreement among competitors.
ww.A store offering a coupon: Offering a coupon is a store's own promotion and is not an agreement with rivals, so it is not price fixing.
ww.A supplier raising costs: A supplier raising its own costs is an independent business decision, not an agreement among competitors to set prices.

rw: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 is the main federal law against monopolies and conspiracies such as price fixing that restrain trade.

ww.The Fair Labor Standards Act: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules, so it does not deal with monopolies or price fixing.
ww.The Clean Water Act of 1972: The Clean Water Act of 1972 regulates water pollution and has nothing to do with competition or monopolies.
ww.The Truth in Savings Act: The Truth in Savings Act requires banks to disclose deposit account terms and rates and does not concern monopolies.

rw: Product liability is the legal responsibility of makers and sellers for injuries or damage caused by defective or unsafe products.

ww.A buyer's duty to pay the seller on time: A buyer's duty to pay the seller is a contract obligation, whereas product liability is a seller's responsibility for harm.
ww.A rule about the size of store shelves: Shelf size is a store design matter and has nothing to do with legal responsibility for harm from products.
ww.A tax on all products sold in stores: A tax on products sold is a sales or excise tax, whereas product liability concerns responsibility for harm from defects.

rw: A company that finds a dangerous defect should notify customers and recall the product to prevent injuries, and it often must report the hazard to regulators.

ww.Wait for a lawsuit to be filed first: Waiting for a lawsuit lets more people get hurt and increases legal exposure, so a responsible company acts at once.
ww.Blame customers for misusing the item: Blaming customers for misuse avoids responsibility when the product itself is defective, and it does not protect people from injury.
ww.Keep selling it quietly and avoid bad pr: Continuing to sell a dangerous product quietly is unethical and illegal, and it exposes the firm to heavy liability.

rw: Recalling the toys and informing the public protects children from the choking hazard and is the ethical choice even though it costs money.

ww.Ignore it unless there is a complaint: Ignoring a known hazard unless someone complains risks injury to children and is both unethical and a legal exposure.
ww.Change the label only, not the toy: Changing the label only does not remove the choking hazard, so children remain at risk.
ww.Sell the rest of the stock quickly: Selling the remaining stock quickly passes a known hazard on to consumers, which is unethical and likely illegal.

rw: Nepotism is giving jobs or advantages to relatives or close family members regardless of qualifications, which is unfair to other candidates.

ww.Interviewing many candidates: Interviewing many candidates is a fair hiring practice and has nothing to do with favoring relatives.
ww.Hiring on merit and skill: Hiring on merit and skill is the fair standard, and it is the opposite of nepotism.
ww.Promoting by performance: Promoting by performance is based on merit, so it is not nepotism.

rw: Reporting suspected theft to a supervisor or the proper channel is the ethical response, as it gives the company a chance to act.

ww.Take supplies for yourself: Taking supplies for yourself would make you a part of the theft, which is unethical and could cost you your job.
ww.Ignore it and say nothing: Ignoring theft allows it to continue, which is unethical because it harms the company and fails the duty to report wrongdoing.
ww.Tell the customers about it: Telling customers does nothing to solve the problem and is not the right channel for reporting an internal issue.

rw: Time theft is getting paid for hours not actually worked, such as arriving late, leaving early, extending breaks or doing personal tasks on the clock.

ww.Working overtime with prior approval: Working overtime with approval is paid work that is properly authorized, so it is not time theft.
ww.Taking approved vacation days each year: Taking approved vacation days is a benefit that the employee earned, so it is not time theft.
ww.Using a lunch break at its set time: Using a lunch break at its scheduled time follows the rules, so it is not time theft.

rw: Honesty builds trust with customers, employees and partners, which leads to loyalty, repeat business and long-term success.

ww.It replaces the need for contracts: Honesty does not remove the need for contracts, since written agreements still protect both sides.
ww.It guarantees the top price in each sale: Honesty does not guarantee a top price in each sale, because prices are set by the market and negotiation.
ww.It removes all competition in a market: Honesty does not remove competition; competitors still exist, but honest firms build reputations that help them compete.

rw: Leaders build an ethical culture by modeling ethical behavior themselves and holding everyone accountable, since employees follow the example set at the top.

ww.Avoiding discussion of ethics in the com: Avoiding talk of ethics sends the signal that it is unimportant, so it would weaken an ethical culture rather than build one.
ww.Rewarding results at any cost to the peo: Rewarding results at any cost encourages cutting corners and misconduct, which damages the ethical culture of a company.
ww.Telling employees to follow rules the le: Telling employees to follow rules that leaders ignore creates hypocrisy and cynicism, which erodes ethical standards.

rw: Pay based only on volume rewards sales numbers, not honesty, which tempts salespeople to overpromise to close deals.

ww.Customers wanting less service from sale: Customers generally want accurate information and good service, so reduced service demand is not a likely reason for the overpromising.
ww.Higher taxes on the whole sales team: Taxes on the sales team do not explain why they exaggerate to customers, since the behavior is tied to how they are paid.
ww.Too much training in ethics each year: Ethics training discourages overpromising, so too much of it would not be the likely cause.

rw: The triple bottom line measures a company's success by profit, people and planet, covering financial, social and environmental results.

ww.Three tax returns filed by a company: The triple bottom line is not about tax returns; it is a framework for measuring a company's social and environmental performance as well as profit.
ww.Three bank accounts for each firm: It has nothing to do with bank accounts; it is a framework that measures success on three dimensions.
ww.Three products for each customer: The triple bottom line is not about products per customer, since it is a measurement framework for profit, people and planet.

rw: Ethical sourcing means buying from suppliers that treat workers fairly, pay fair wages, ensure safe conditions and avoid forced labor or environmental harm.

ww.Using forced labor to cut the costs of m: Forced labor is a serious human rights abuse, so using it to cut costs is the opposite of ethical sourcing.
ww.Hiding supplier names from the buyers an: Hiding supplier names avoids accountability, whereas ethical sourcing involves transparency about where products come from.
ww.Choosing suppliers by the lowest price,: Choosing only by lowest price ignores how suppliers treat workers and the environment, so it is not ethical sourcing.

rw: Fair trade is a system that pays producers, often in developing countries, a fair price and promotes safe working conditions and sustainable practices.

ww.A system with a fixed profit for every r: Fair trade does not guarantee a fixed profit for retailers; it focuses on fair pay and conditions for producers.
ww.A system of free products given to buyer: Fair trade does not mean giving away free products; buyers still pay, and part of the price supports producers.
ww.A system that bans all international tra: Fair trade is not a ban on international trade; it supports trade conducted on fair terms with developing-country producers.

rw: Reporting an error that cost a sale but misled a customer puts honesty ahead of short-term gain, which shows prioritizing ethics.

ww.Quitting without telling anyone about th: Quitting without telling anyone avoids the problem rather than fixing it, so it does not show prioritizing ethics.
ww.Hiding the error to keep the sale, since: Hiding the error to keep the sale puts short-term gain over honesty and misleads the customer, so it is unethical.
ww.Blaming a coworker for the error that wa: Blaming a coworker for the error is dishonest and unfair, and it puts self-protection ahead of ethics.

rw: An export is a good or service produced in one country and sold to a buyer in another country, which brings money into the exporting country.

ww.A good or service bought from another co: A good or service bought from another country is an import, which is the opposite of an export.
ww.A tax on goods that cross the border int: A tax on goods crossing the border is a tariff or duty, not an export, which is the sale itself.
ww.A limit on goods that are allowed in fro: A limit on goods allowed in from abroad is an import quota, a trade barrier, and not an export.
